what_it_does: Large language models (LLMs — AI systems that generate text) are normally run on power-hungry server GPUs, but researchers want to run smaller versions on cheap, low-power edge devices like the Xilinx ZCU102 FPGA (a reconfigurable chip drawing under 10 watts). The bottleneck is that such devices have very limited memory bandwidth — data can't flow in fast enough to feed the computation — and naive approaches waste bandwidth by repeatedly writing big intermediate results to slow external memory (DRAM). MEADOW cuts these wasted memory trips using two complementary tricks: a new order of operations that keeps intermediate results alive in fast on-chip registers, and a compressed weight format that transmits only the unique chunks of the model's parameters.
method_in_detail:
The problem. Running an LLM at edge requires two phases: a prefill phase (processing the user's prompt all at once) and a decode phase (generating one new word at a time). The attention computation — the part where every word checks how relevant it is to every other word — produces large intermediate matrices that standard approaches dump to external DRAM and reload repeatedly. At 1–12 Gbps of bandwidth (typical for these low-power FPGAs, versus 900+ Gbps on datacenter GPUs), this repeated reading and writing dominates latency.

Trick 1: Token-Parallel Head-Sequential (TPHS) dataflow. In standard operation, all attention heads for all tokens are handled together using one big matrix-multiply loop (called GEMM — a generalized matrix multiplication). MEADOW instead pipelines the stages within a single attention head across multiple tokens simultaneously: while token 1's query vector flows into the softmax stage (a normalization step that turns raw scores into probabilities), token 2's query is still being computed, and their intermediate values pass directly through fast on-chip pipeline registers rather than going out to DRAM. This eliminates the expensive store-then-reload of intermediate attention outputs entirely during the Q/QKT/softmax/weighted-sum stages.

Trick 2: Weight packing. The model's weight matrices (its learned parameters) must still be fetched from DRAM once per output token. MEADOW analyzes the quantized weights (already rounded to 8-bit integers) and finds that many small chunks of the matrix are identical — in the OPT-125M model, the reduction ratio (unique chunks vs. total chunks) is 100- to 1000-fold. It stores only the unique chunks plus an index table. Before transmission, it assigns shorter bit codes to more frequent chunk IDs (frequency-aware reindexing) and packs multiple encoded indices into each memory transaction at variable precision (packet-specific encoding), so bandwidth is used more efficiently.

The result. On the ZCU102 FPGA, MEADOW achieves 2.5× lower prefill latency and 1.5× lower decode latency versus naive GEMM, and over 40% lower end-to-end latency versus prior FPGA LLM optimization approaches, with no loss in model accuracy.
